heading: CHAPTER XVII.
title: CONCERNING CRUELTY AND CLEMENCY, AND WHETHER IT IS BETTER TO BE LOVED THAN FEARED
exclusions: front matter and dedication before THE PRINCE
notes: Chapter 17 argues that a few hard examples can be more merciful than soft indulgence that lets murders, robberies, and disorder spread through the whole people.

The chapter's central distinction is fear without hatred: safer feared than loved when one must choose, but still avoid hatred by acting with manifest cause and by abstaining from subjects' property and women.
The military section clarifies the argument by contrasting Hannibal's discipline-producing cruelty with Scipio's over-forbearance.
